alt: Unit 1 has 60 marks: Section A on families (40 marks) and Section B on research methods (20 marks). The same research methods and theory content is examined in Unit 1 through short and structured questions and in Unit 2 through one extended response.
caption: Research methods and theory content is examined in both Units 1 and 2.

alt: Six cards: extended, nuclear and single-parent families; non-family living arrangements such as communes, living alone and foster care; cultural variation including Therborn’s typology; and arranged marriage, love marriage and monogamy.
caption: Family forms and marriage practices vary within and between societies.

alt: Functionalists such as Parsons study family functions and the fit of the nuclear family; Marxists such as Engels see the family serving capitalism; feminists such as Oakley study how families shape gender positions.
caption: Each perspective asks whom the family serves.

alt: Demographic factors such as birth and death rates, migration and ageing, together with industrialisation, urbanisation, personal life and individualisation, produce newer family types such as sandwich-generation, blended, living-apart-together, beanpole and transnational families.
caption: Demographic and social change explain the growth of family diversity.

alt: Gendered roles are shown as the male breadwinner or instrumental role and the female expressive role. The triple shift combines paid work, domestic work and emotional work, alongside themes such as power, violence, child-centredness and boomerang families.
caption: The triple shift adds emotional work to paid and domestic work.

alt: A grid comparing positivist methods, which are reliable and generalisable but may lack validity, with interpretivist methods, which are valid and in-depth but less reliable. Practical, ethical and theoretical factors and six sampling methods are listed beneath.
caption: Reliability and validity often trade off against each other.

alt: Strengths of participant observation for studying a gang, such as validity, access and insight into meanings, set against weaknesses such as low reliability, small samples, going native, ethical risks and cost.
caption: Assess a method against the research aim, not in the abstract.
